title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a false match from an automated system, not a mistaken officer. The Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, and Kansas has more than 100 plate designs, about half of them specialty, so one number can belong to more than one plate. The system treats a plate number as an identifier of a single vehicle, and in Kansas it is not one.

The failure sits at the point where a camera alert turns into a police stop. In Colwich an officer recognised the minivan and learned the wrong plate type had been entered, so a person caught the error before it went further. In Catoosa the alert reached officers without that correction and the stop was made at gunpoint. Catching it would have taken a check that the number was unique, or a verification of plate type and background before officers acted, and Captain Casey Slaughter said camera alerts alone are not enough for a stop while wrong entries can force officers to act.

It is not established that the camera vendor or any police agency broke a rule or acted unlawfully, and the account rests on a single outlet's investigation. Kansas is moving from six digit to seven digit, nonduplicated plate numbers, which changes the underlying duplication but is not a finding about this incident.

reports.title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

summary:
Matthew and Leah Spurlock were pulled over because their Kansas KU Alumni license plate number, 7007, matched a stolen GMC pickup's temporary tag. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock camera alerted police to a possible stolen vehicle, but an officer recognized their minivan and learned the wrong plate type had been entered. About a month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another Flock camera led police to stop them at gunpoint and handcuff Matthew before the mistake was sorted out.

Wichita police Captain Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, and Kansas has more than 100 plate designs, about half specialty, so numbers can be duplicated. He said camera alerts alone are not enough for a stop, but wrong entries can force officers to act. Kansas is moving from six digit to seven digit, nonduplicated plate numbers. The Spurlocks are no longer worried because the stolen vehicle entry has expired, and they hope to keep their 14 year old plate.
